title: Role of the trombone and old-time trombone soloists
summary: Trombone 'tore paper' with long slide notes in the old days; Willie Cornish is named as someone who took many solos.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: But when the clarinet player would be up there?
Well then you could take down, or otherwise play variations with that clarinet.
Would the trombone be playing at the same time? At the same time, yeah, yeah, yeah.

In other words he'd be tearing paper just making those long notes, you know, we call that tearing paper, you know. Ta, ta. They'd take those hearts like they take today now. And the trombone players play almost like a trumpet player today, make all those variations today, you know. At that time they didn't. Just a long slide note, you know, filling in. That's what it was. Very few trombone players take a solo at the time, but most of the time all during the pieces fill in that part, you know. Fill in these parts. It's a lot. It was to blend with the rest of the music, blend together.
Who did they have that could take a solo on trombone good in those days? Huh?
They told me there's so many, they all thought they were good, you know. And did they take many of them?
Who would feature himself much on trombone? A lot of old men, I just can't call names.
What about Frankie Dooson, would he? Or would he play mostly in the ensemble? Frankie, Frankie.
You don't remember Frankie? No, I'm trying to think now. You called him Frankie Dooson. Not Frank, Frank.
We knew what he was in the name. I'm talking about.
Willie Cornish, did you know him? Cornish, Cornish, yeah. Big Cornish.
Yeah, yeah. Did he take many solos? Yeah, most all of them take me solo. They were now.
Oh yeah. In the old days.
In other words, every time. You know what we call it, every time. Each man had to hold that chair.
